paragraphs.text: Mitochondrial myopathy with lactic acidosis is an autosomal recessive disorder caused by biallelic loss-of-function variants in PNPLA8, which encodes calcium-independent phospholipase A2-gamma. The first patient reported with PNPLA8 variants had progressive muscle weakness, loss of ambulation, lactic acidosis, dystonia, seizures, and abnormal mitochondrial ultrastructure in muscle (Saunders et al., 2015). Later reports showed that PNPLA8-related disease is a phenotypic continuum. At the severe end are a developmental and/or degenerative epileptic-dyskinetic encephalopathy with congenital microcephaly and pontocerebellar hypoplasia; at the mild end is a childhood- or later-onset neurodegeneration with movement disorder and cerebellar atrophy (Abdel-Hamid et al., 2024; Nakamura et al., 2024).

paragraphs.text: Mastaglia et al. (1980) described a 23-year-old man with a mitochondrial myopathy. He had had a high-output circulatory state and cardiomyopathy, which caused cardiac insufficiency 22 years before the skeletal myopathy appeared. Venous lactate levels were elevated, and severe lactic acidosis developed at one stage of the illness. Electron microscopy of muscle showed various mitochondrial abnormalities and an accumulation of neutral lipids, which was confirmed histochemically and by thin-layer chromatography.

paragraphs.text: Saunders et al. (2015) reported a girl (CMH193) who began toe-walking in her first year. She had a positive Gowers sign at age 2 years and could no longer walk by age 3 years. She had fatigue, declining fine motor skills, dysarthria, progressive proximal muscle weakness, tight heel cords, rightward deviation of the tongue, dysmetria, hypotonia, spasticity, and dystonia, including oral motor dystonia. She had complex partial seizures with left temporal lobe spikes on EEG. Her body habitus was very lean and she did not gain weight. She had lactic acidosis that required bicarbonate, an elevated anion gap, elevated blood pyruvate, and cerebrospinal fluid 5-methyltetrahydrofolate deficiency. Brain MRI showed increased signal intensity of the medial globus pallidus. Muscle biopsy showed variable fiber size with atrophic fibers but no ragged red fibers. Electron microscopy showed disarray of mitochondrial cristae, osmiophilic mitochondrial inclusions, subsarcolemmal aggregates of abnormal mitochondria, and increased secondary lysosomes. Creatine phosphokinase was not elevated, the lactate:pyruvate ratio was not elevated, and no electron transport chain defect was found. She was last reported at age 7 years.

paragraphs.text: Patient 2 of Shukla et al. (2018), of Indian/Fijian origin and born to nonconsanguineous parents, developed normally until about 1 year of age. Regression began at 13 months, with epilepsia partialis continua and focal seizures. At last report, at age 15 years, she had severe global developmental delay, was nonverbal, and was fed by gastrostomy. She had central hypotonia, acquired microcephaly, choreiform movements, dystonia, progressive proximal muscle weakness, absent muscle stretch reflexes, spasticity, and evolving severe contractures of the hamstrings, biceps, and ankles. Brain imaging showed prominent ventricles, delayed myelination, progressive cerebellar atrophy, brainstem atrophy, parietal and occipital cortical volume loss, and thinning of the corpus callosum. MR spectroscopy showed an elevated lipid-lactate peak in the parenchyma and cerebrospinal fluid. EEG showed multifocal epileptiform discharges with background slowing, and visual evoked potentials were of reduced amplitude with prolonged latency. She also had hypertrophic cardiomyopathy, subaortic stenosis, elevated blood lactate, elevated growth and differentiation factor-15, obstructive sleep apnea, and restrictive lung disease. Electron microscopy of muscle showed enlarged, irregularly shaped mitochondria surrounded by membrane whorls, with disrupted cristae, electron-dense deposits, lipid droplets, pools of glycogen, and empty vacuoles. Activities of electron transport chain complexes I through IV were within normal ranges. The authors noted that her presentation resembled that of the patient reported by Saunders et al. (2015).

paragraphs.text: Burnyte et al. (2023) described a milder, adolescence-onset form of PNPLA8-associated disease in 2 sibs. The brother (sibling A), age 49 years at last report, developed lower limb weakness and distal muscle atrophy at age 14 years. He had ataxia with axial ataxia and dysmetria, tetraparesis, decreased muscle tone, wasting of the calf and foot muscles, absent lower limb tendon reflexes, foot deformities, bilateral Babinski signs, and length-dependent hypoesthesia of the lower limbs. Studies showed a sensorimotor axonal polyneuropathy. He became nonambulant at age 44 years. At age 45 years he had mild dysarthria and horizontal nystagmus, and brain imaging showed mild cerebellar atrophy. His sister (sibling B) developed difficulty walking and lower limb weakness at age 14 years. At age 21 years she had muscle atrophy in the distal upper and lower limbs, absent lower limb tendon reflexes, bilateral Babinski signs, severe axial ataxia, and appendicular dysmetria that was more marked in the lower limbs, and she could not maintain an upright posture. She had an axonal sensorimotor polyneuropathy, and EMG showed abnormal spontaneous activity in distal lower limb muscles without myopathic changes. Cranial nerve examination and cognition were normal in both sibs. Cerebellar ataxia and polyneuropathy progressed markedly in the teens but only slightly in adulthood. Neither sib had visual, auditory, cardiac, or liver involvement.

paragraphs.text: Nakamura et al. (2024) analyzed 14 new and 11 previously reported individuals with biallelic PNPLA8 variants. Eight patients from families 1 through 8 formed a severe group. Their ancestries were Japanese (families 1 and 2, both nonconsanguineous), Saudi Arabian, Iraqi, Afghan, Pakistani, Turkish, and Lebanese (families 3-8, all consanguineous); families 7 and 8 had been reported previously. Common features in this group were congenital microcephaly (5 of 7), global developmental delay with no milestones attained (7 of 7), peripheral spasticity (7 of 8), and seizures beginning by 7 months of age (8 of 8), with onset as early as day 1. Most of these patients also had progressive microcephaly, severe intellectual disability, and hypotonia. Dystonia was present in 2 of the 6 patients with data (patients 1 and 2). Imaging showed a simplified gyral pattern, pontocerebellar hypoplasia, and cerebral and/or cerebellar atrophy. Patient 1 died at age 4 years, patient 2 at age 10 months, and patient 8 at age 8 months.

paragraphs.text: Nakamura et al. (2024) described a milder group of 4 patients: 3 Iranian sibs from a consanguineous family (family 11; patients 11a, 11b, and 11c, ages 33 and 29 years for 11a and 11c) and a 21-year-old Egyptian woman from a consanguineous family (patient 12). All 4 attained walking (4 of 4) and later had regression of milestones (4 of 4). Three had ataxia (3 of 4), 3 had mild or no intellectual disability (3 of 4), and seizures were single or absent (4 of 4); patient 11b had a seizure at age 31 years. They had a late-onset movement disorder with dystonia, along with hypotonia and a neuromuscular disorder. Brain MRI showed little or no cerebral cortical volume loss but progressive cerebellar atrophy. The authors concluded that PNPLA8-related neurologic disease forms a continuum, from a variable developmental and/or degenerative epileptic-dyskinetic encephalopathy with congenital microcephaly and pontocerebellar hypoplasia to childhood- or later-onset neurodegeneration with movement disorder and cerebellar atrophy.

paragraphs.text: Nakamura et al. (2024) identified 14 PNPLA8 variants in their patients, 12 of them novel: 4 nonsense, 5 frameshift, 3 intronic variants near exon-intron boundaries, and 2 missense. Each variant had a population frequency below 0.001%. Twelve of the 14 individuals carried combinations of nonsense, frameshift, and splice-site variants, which suggested loss of function. In lymphoblastoid cells from patient 1, the c.1625+3_1625+6del variant caused skipping of exons 6 through 8. Immunoblotting of his skin fibroblasts showed a significant reduction in the 77-kDa PNPLA8 protein, indicating a null effect, and a similar null effect was found for the p.Glu296LysfsTer6 variant in patient 6. Patient-derived cells were not available to test c.2075-2A-G (patient 2) and c.1684-2A-G (patient 5) experimentally, but SpliceAI predicted that each causes loss of a splice acceptor site (delta scores 0.97 and 0.93, respectively). Patient 12, who was homozygous for p.Leu759AlafsTer4, showed weak expression of the 77-kDa protein, which suggested residual function. Skin fibroblasts from a previously reported patient with a severe phenotype who was homozygous for the missense variant p.Val520Asp expressed PNPLA8 protein at levels similar to controls. In patient fibroblasts, cardiolipin and monolysocardiolipin levels appeared lower than in controls but did not correlate significantly with phenotypic severity.

paragraphs.text: In a Japanese boy (patient 1) from a nonconsanguineous family, Nakamura et al. (2024) identified a c.1625+3_1625+6del variant in the PNPLA8 gene. He had congenital and progressive microcephaly, seizures from day 1, no developmental milestones, spasticity, dystonia, a simplified gyral pattern, pontocerebellar hypoplasia, and cerebral and cerebellar atrophy, and he died at age 4 years. In his lymphoblastoid cells the variant caused skipping of exons 6 through 8 owing to aberrant splicing. Immunoblotting of his skin fibroblasts showed a significant reduction in the 77-kDa PNPLA8 protein, indicating a null effect, and maximal mitochondrial respiration in the fibroblasts was reduced.
